t:
The Act entitled “An Act to provide for the establishment of the Lowell National Historical Park in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, and for other purposes” approved June 5, 1978 (Public Law 95–290; 92 Stat. 290; 16 U.S.C. 410cc et seq.) is amended as follows:
    (1) In section 101(a), by adding a new paragraph after paragraph (2) as follows:“(3) The boundaries of the park are modified to include five parcels of land identified on the map entitled ‘Boundary Adjustment, Lowell National Historical Park,’ numbered 475/81,424B and dated September 2004, and as delineated in section 202(a)(2)(G).”. 
    (2) In section 202(a)(2), by adding at the end the following new subparagraph:“(G) The properties shown on the map identified in subsection (101)(a)(3) as follows:“(i) 91 Pevey Street.“(ii) The portion of 607 Middlesex Place.“(iii) Eagle Court.“(iv) The portion of 50 Payne Street.“(v) 726 Broadway.”.

fable.w: This section only amends the Lowell National Historical Park statute to modify the park boundaries and list five added parcels. Congress makes the boundary change directly, with no comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking, consultation with state or local entities, or right to sue. The tempting reading is that a park boundary adjustment affecting local property implies local involvement, but the text provides no process for any party outside the federal government.

opus.w: This section changes the Lowell National Historical Park boundaries to add five listed parcels. It does not provide for consultation, hearings, public comment, advisory bodies, rulemaking or a right to sue by anyone outside the federal government. Adding land might suggest that owners or local governments were involved, but the text itself creates no such process.
